# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“OBED—Obed—what’s wrong? Are you ill, Obed?”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0000 }

Thirza was the one who uttered the words, her hurried speech betraying her fear. Holding an armful of white narcissus—a flower whose appearance and scent Nell would be unable to enjoy for a very long time—Nell walked through the hall, arriving just as Thirza spoke and in time to catch sight of Obed in the doorway of the porch, holding a piece of paper that was folded, his countenance unnaturally tense and pale. Dropping the blooms, Nell rushed through the kitchen toward him simultaneously with Thirza. Neither of them made it in time; Obed collapsed over the doorway before either could get to him.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0001 }

“He has passed out,” Thirza uttered breathlessly. “Nell, hurry to fetch Martin—fast, fast! The barn is where he can be found.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0002 }

Having just returned from the post office by car, Martin, the hired man, immediately set off to fetch the doctor, stopping by Pear Hill as he went to tell Mr. and Mrs. Pembroke to go over. Mrs. Sowerby, who happened to be visiting there on an errand, accompanied them. Upon their arrival, they discovered Nell and Thirza frantically attempting to bring Obed back to consciousness.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0003 }

Mrs. Sowerby eased them out of the way softly, checked his pulse, and subsequently placed her ear against his heart. Mournfully, she gazed at their worried faces as tears filled her eyes.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0004 }

“Oh, Thirza,” she uttered with seriousness. “I am not sure—there is anything we can do to help him.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0005 }

“Mrs. Sowerby, you do not believe—you are unable to believe Obed has become—has become—” The horrific term was impossible for Nell to utter; a feeling of nausea came over her, and her face grew pale.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0006 }

“Child, yes, it frightens me. Observe his expression. You will understand its meaning once you’ve witnessed that expression as frequently as I have.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0007 }

Nell gazed upon the motionless countenance, observing there the stamp of the Great Presence.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0008 }

The physician arrived and stated that a swift, likely painless shock had almost certainly brought about immediate death. This shock’s underlying cause was found within the document Obed had possessed, the very paper Martin had carried from the office earlier that day. A report detailed within it disclosed that the Abbey Bank had failed.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0009 }

Brierley rapidly learned the news, and throughout the day acquaintances and locals packed into Grey Shutters, arriving and departing to perform thoughtful acts for both the deceased and the survivors. For the very first time, the timid, reserved Obed Abernethy became the focus of main attention; the pale grandeur of mortality had descended upon him, distinguishing him like someone who had been crowned.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0010 }

As a peaceful evening gently descended upon Grey Shutters, silence and tranquility settled upon the ancient residence. Resting within his casket in the parlor was Obed Abernethy, with his extended silver locks encircling a serene countenance that bore a gentle, affectionate grin, appearing as though he were merely asleep and experiencing agreeable visions. Blossoms surrounded him—charming, traditional blooms that his mother had set in the farmstead garden during her early married life, and toward which Obed had forever harbored a quiet, unspoken affection. Nell had collected the blooms and delivered them to him, her tormented, dry eyes glowing against her pale countenance. Doing this represented the final act she was able to perform on his behalf.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0011 }

The night was spent in their company by Mrs. Sowerby and the Pembrokes. Approaching the east gable, in which a position at her window was occupied by Nell, Isolde remarked softly:
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0012 }

“Would it please you, dear Nell, if I stayed in your room tonight?”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0013 }

“Thank you, Isolde.” Nell gazed with deep sincerity at her friend. “I believe you will not take it the wrong way if I tell you that I desire solitude. Fear does not bother me. Not a single minute of solitude has been mine since the event—and it is what I desire. My wish is to remain entirely silent and still so I can attempt to comprehend it. Understanding it is beyond me. Half of the time I feel that Obed could not possibly be deceased; whereas the other half makes it feel as though his death occurred ages ago and this dreadful, numb pain has stayed with me ever since.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0014 }

Isolde failed to comprehend fully. She was able to grasp Thirza’s fiery sorrow, which breached every limit of innate restraint and daily routine in its tempestuous surge, more easily than Nell’s unweeping anguish. Nevertheless, she departed gently, abandoning Nell to observe her initial watch with grief in solitude.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0015 }

Nell wished that her weeping might happen while she was alone. To her, it felt like an awful truth that she was unable to weep a single tear for Obed, a person she had held so dear and who had shown her such kindness, Obed who had strolled beside her yesterday evening when the sun set and was currently resting in the shadowed chamber beneath with that terrifying calmness upon his forehead. Yet at the start no tears arrived, not even as she got down on her knees near her window in the dark and offered prayers, gazing toward the stars past the hills—there were no tears, merely that identical dreadful, numb throbbing of grief that continued to throb until fatigue from the day's suffering and commotion caused her to drift off to sleep.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0016 }

During the night she woke up, surrounded by the quiet and the dark, and the memory of the day washed over her like a surge of grief. Before her eyes, Obed’s face appeared smiling at her just as he had done when they said goodbye at the gate on that final evening—his voice reached her ears saying, “My girl—my girl that I’m proud of.” At that moment tears arrived and Nell cried her heart out. Hearing her, Thirza sneaked inside to soothe her.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0017 }

“There—there—do not weep in such a way, dearie. Doing so will not restore him. It—it—is wrong to weep in such a way. That was clear to me today, though I was unable to stop myself at the time. To me, he was ever a brother so good and kind—yet God understands what is best.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0018 }

“Oh, Thirza, simply allow me to weep,” Nell cried out. “That pain was worse than these tears are. Remain by my side briefly and hold your arm about me—like this. I was unable to let Isolde remain, even though she is sweet and kind and good—however, this grief is not hers—she stands apart from it and was incapable of drawing near enough to my heart to assist me. This grief belongs to us—to you and to me. Oh, Thirza, how shall we manage in his absence?”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0019 }

“Nell, we still have one another. If you were not with me—had you never arrived—I cannot imagine what my plight would be. Oh, Nell, perhaps I have been somewhat stern and severe toward you, as I am well aware—yet despite that, you must never believe my love for you was any less than Obed's. While the opportunity remains, I wish to speak these words to you. Expressing the feelings in my heart has always proved difficult for me, though such moments make it less so. My love for you is as deep as though you were my very own child, and from the moment you arrived at Grey Shutters, you have brought me nothing but happiness and solace.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0020 }

Two days later, Obed Abernethy was borne across the doorway of his homestead, leaving behind the fields he had worked, the orchards he had cherished, and the trees he had planted; following this, Brierley returned to its customary quietness, and even within Grey Shutters things drifted back into their former routine, with tasks performed and obligations met as routinely as ever, despite the constant, painful feeling of “loss in all familiar things.” Unaccustomed to sorrow, Nell felt it was nearly tragic that life could continue this way—that their existence could proceed normally without Obed. A feeling akin to shame and guilt came over her upon realizing that the fir-framed sunrises and the unfolding soft pink garden buds still brought her the same old surge of joy—that she enjoyed Isolde’s calls and was brought to laughter and smiles by Isolde’s cheerful language and demeanor—that, in short, the lovely realm of blooms, affection, and comradeship remained fully capable of delighting her imagination and stirring her soul, and that life continued to summon her with numerous demanding calls.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0021 }

“It somehow feels as though I am being disloyal to Obed by enjoying these matters now that he is no longer here,” she remarked with longing to Mrs. Wace during an evening they spent alongside one another in the manse garden. “I am missing him terribly—constantly—and nevertheless, Mrs. Wace, the world and existence appear extremely lovely and fascinating to me despite everything. Today Isolde uttered a humorous remark and I caught myself laughing. At the time it occurred, I believed laughter would never be possible for me again. And somehow it feels as if I should not.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0022 }

“While Obed was present, listening to your laughter gave him joy, and he was glad to see you enjoying the nice things about you,” Mrs. Wace remarked softly. “He is merely absent at present; and he still appreciates knowing that very same thing. I feel certain that we ought not to close our hearts to the restorative remedies that nature provides to us. Nevertheless, your emotion is understandable to me. It seems to me that everyone goes through that very experience. We feel indignation at the idea that any object can bring us joy when a person we cherish is absent to partake in that joy alongside us, and it feels nearly as though we are being disloyal to our grief whenever we notice our enthusiasm for living coming back to us.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0023 }

“This afternoon, I went down to the cemetery so I could place a rosebush on the grave of Obed,” Nell remarked lost in thought. “A cutting from that small white Scotch rosebush which his mother had brought with her from Scotland a long time ago was what I brought; Obed had always preferred those particular roses above all others—they were remarkably tiny and sweet on their prickly stalks. Planted next to his resting place, it brought me a sense of joy—just as though carrying it there to be close to him was a deed that boundly pleased him. In heaven, I hope he is provided with roses just like those. It may be that the spirits of every one of those small white roses he cherished through so many summers gathered to greet his arrival. Right now, I have to return home. Thirza is completely by herself, and as the twilight falls, she becomes lonely.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0024 }

“I am afraid she will experience even greater loneliness when you depart once more for college,” Mrs. Wace remarked.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0025 }

Nell offered no response; stating good night, she walked back to Grey Shutters at a deliberate pace. Thirza occupied a spot on the front door-steps, and Nell took a seat next to her. Unlocked and open behind their backs, the door was secured by a large pink conch shell that displayed traces of oceanic sunsets within its polished interior spirals.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0026 }

Nell picked a few sprigs of pale-yellow honeysuckle and placed them in her hair. She enjoyed the delightful trace of scent that hung above her like an airy blessing whenever she made a movement.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0027 }

“While you were out, Doctor Tranter stopped by,” Thirza stated. “The specialist is arriving in town tomorrow, according to him, and he is adamant that I need to go get my eyes checked. I guess I ought to go and get it done with. If that man is able to provide me with the proper glasses for my eyes, I will be deeply grateful. Will it be alright for you to remain here by yourself while I am gone? I will need Martin to take me there, and there is ironing as well as baking that needs doing.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0028 }

“I am going to be fine. Isolde is going to drop by so that I have company. I am going to manage the baking and ironing wonderfully—there is no need to worry about me starching the handkerchiefs or putting liniment in the cake as flavoring.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0029 }

Thirza chuckled.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0030 }

“Nell, back then you had such a knack for committing blunders. You were perpetually landing yourself in trouble. I truly used to believe a demon had hold of you. Can you recall when you gave your hair a different color?”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0031 }

“Certainly, that is true. It will stay in my memory forever,” Nell murmured with a smile, reaching up to feel the thick plaited coil arranged around her finely formed head. “Occasionally these days I find it slightly amusing to recall how much I used to fret over my hair—though it is rarely a laughing matter to me, as it caused me genuine distress back then. Both my freckles and my hair brought me immense misery. The freckles have actually disappeared; furthermore, others are kind enough to describe my hair as auburn these days—everyone except Flossie Tulk. Just yesterday, she told me she felt it was actually more red than it used to be, or that my dark attire at least accentuated the redness, before inquiring whether individuals with red hair ever become accustomed to possessing it. Thirza, I am nearly on the verge of abandoning my attempts to fond of Flossie Tulk. My endeavors to care for her have been what I previously would have considered brave, yet Flossie Tulk refuses to let herself be liked.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0032 }

“Since Flossie belongs to the Tulk family,” Thirza remarked tartly, “her unpleasant behavior is simply in her nature. Although I imagine such individuals fulfill a helpful role in the community, I have to admit that their function eludes me just as much as the function of thistles does. Will Flossie be working as a teacher?”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0033 }

“No, she is returning to Regent’s the following year. Elias Purdy and Wilfred Mott are doing the same. Odette and Opal intend to teach, having both secured positions—Odette in Stonebridge and Opal in a location farther west.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0034 }

“Isn’t Hugh Carrow also going to be teaching?”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0035 }

“Yes”—concisely.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0036 }

“He is such a handsome man,” Thirza remarked vaguely. “During last Sunday’s service I noticed him, and he appeared remarkably tall and manly. His resemblance to his father when he was that age is striking. John Carrow was a lovely youth. He and I were truly close friends back then. People referred to him as my beau.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0037 }

Nell raised her eyes, showing immediate interest.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0038 }

“Oh, Thirza—and what was the outcome?—for what reason failed you to—”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0039 }

“An argument occurred between us. When he requested my forgiveness, I refused to give it. I intended to do so eventually—yet I remained moody and furious, desiring to discipline him beforehand. He failed to return—a strong streak of independence ran through the Carrows. Still, a sense of regret always stayed with me. A part of me consistently wished that I had granted him forgiveness while the opportunity existed.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0040 }

“Then a touch of romance has entered your life as well,” Nell murmured gently.
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0041 }

“Yes, I imagine it could be named as such. Looking at me, you would not believe it, would you? However, judging individuals by their appearances is never reliable. Everyone has erased John and me from memory. I had even failed to remember it on my own. Yet, seeing Hugh this past Sunday brought the whole thing returning to my mind.”
{: #nw-v01-c37-p0042 }
